text: The men called up to defend the country are not soldiers and not young. An old man issues the summons, volunteers assemble, and an enemy arrives from outside with no face and no stated demand; that is the entire mechanism, and Hugo Santiago gives it two hours. The science-fiction label sits oddly, since nothing here needs a future. What the premise needs is waiting: positions taken, assignments handed out, the ordinary business of people who have agreed to stand somewhere without being told for how long. Argentina, 1969. The Museo del Cine survey of Argentine cinema lists it. The invaders stay abstract. The defenders grow more particular by the scene, down to the fatigue of men doing at fifty what is generally asked of the young.

Foreign carmakers were settling into Brazil, the plants went up, and Carlos took a job in São Paulo. He is good at it: manager at a parts factory, a salary that covers the apartment and the marriage, a life he did not exactly choose. Luiz Sérgio Person made the film in 1965, while all of that was still new. The pressure in it is not failure. Carlos succeeds. The orders come in, the money is real, and none of it touches what he wants touched. A hundred and nine minutes of competence and dissatisfaction could be airless. It is not, because the factory floor, the manager's office and the household stay in one frame of reference, so the discontent has an address rather than a mood.

Five boys come down from the favela with peanuts to sell and the whole of Rio to cross. The day is punishing, the stock is small, and every district they reach has its own crowd, its own prices and its own manner toward a child holding a bag, which is how Nelson Pereira dos Santos gets a portrait of a city out of an errand. Ninety-one minutes, five routes, one hot afternoon. The boys are handled as workers and not as objects of pity: quotas, sore feet, the arithmetic of a small sale running underneath whatever else is happening around them. Made in 1955, it puts the poorest people in Rio at the centre and lets everyone else pass through the frame on the way somewhere.

Lúcio Flávio robbed banks and got out of prisons, and enough of Rio enjoyed the performance to make him something close to public property. Héctor Babenco filmed the case in 1976, near enough to the events that the name was known before the lights went down. Two hours: the robberies get their due, the nerve and the timing and the flourishes that got him written about, and then the film turns to the arrangement underneath, the traffic between men committing crimes and men paid to stop them, including the squad that skipped the trial and went straight to the killing. Charm and corruption run on the same current here, and Babenco declines to separate them for anyone's comfort, so admiration and indictment keep arriving in the same scene.

In 1960 a train carrying a payroll crossed Rio de Janeiro and did not arrive with the money. Roberto Farias put the hold-up on screen two years later, with the name of the gang's leader, Tião Medonho, still in circulation. A robbery has to be legible before it can be admired, and the early stretch does that work plainly: the plan, the men, the timetable. Then the harder half. A hundred and two minutes leaves room for what the money does to men who cannot say where it came from, who go on living where they have always lived, among neighbours who notice a new pair of shoes. What it gets right is scale: a large sum turns dangerous fast in a place where everyone knows what everyone earns.

Didi, Dedé, Mussum and Zacarias are minor officials until a circus finds out what they can do to a crowd. Bartolo's tent takes them on, the audiences arrive, the Baron who owns the place starts counting, and a magician billed as Assis Satan does not care to be second on the programme. The Abraccine hundred of Brazilian films includes this, which is worth knowing before the pratfalls begin. A hundred minutes of music, chases and slapstick, aimed at children and unembarrassed about it. The comedy runs on four temperaments grinding against one another rather than on anything the plot supplies, which is why the villains can afford to be simple, and why the proposition underneath stays clear: being loved by a crowd and being paid by one are separate transactions.

Ransom is why the schoolteacher stays alive, and why Galdino Ferreira's band keeps moving her across dry country. Olívia is the captive. Teodoro is the man in the band who makes the mistake of caring, and the captain is cruel in the way of someone whose authority depends on it. Lima Barreto shot this in 1953 and borrowed the western outright, the ride and the ridgeline and the leader whose word is law, then set it among the cangaceiros of the Brazilian Northeast, where the badlands do half the work of an antagonist. A hundred and five minutes, most of them outdoors. A band held together by fear develops a discipline problem the moment one of its men wants something for himself, and that is the fault line the film opens and then follows.

The footage sat for thirteen years because the man who shot it could not work out what he had. Santiago had been the butler in João Moreira Salles's parents' house; in 1992 Salles filmed him at length, then set the material aside, and went back to it only in 2005. Eighty minutes come out of that interval, which is the method: a documentary obliged to account for why it stalled ends up accounting for the house it was shot in, and for the difference in standing between the man behind the camera and the man in front of it. Two subjects, then. One is a peculiar old employee with his own way of holding a room. The other is a filmmaker listening to his younger voice give instructions, and hearing what was already inside the questions.

Soldiers are posted to a food depot with orders to keep the hungry away from it. The town is in the dry Northeast of Brazil, the year is 1964, and the situation is stated so plainly that Ruy Guerra needs only eighty-five minutes. The soldiers are not monsters. They are men with rifles, an assignment and far too much idle time in a place that offers them nothing, while a truck driver who likes them and despises what they are there to do moves between the barracks and the street. Around them a religious figure gives starvation a shape people can act on. Guerra keeps the weapons ordinary, cleaned and carried and propped against walls, so that the subject becomes the interval before anything happens, and how normal an arrangement can look while it holds.

All the wealth in the world, on one condition: that Nazareno Cruz give up the woman he loves. The Mighty One puts it plainly. A curse is said to sit on Nazareno; this is the way around it, and the price is her. Leonardo Favio filmed the bargain in 1975 without irony and without distance; the wolf in the title is not asked to stand in for anything, and the eighty-five minutes go to melodrama at full strength, which is the register the material asks for. Argentina put it forward as its submission to the Academy Awards. The terms are what hold the attention: one party can offer the world and wait as long as it takes, the other has one life and a single thing in it he will not trade.

The night is paid for in advance, and the hours still have to be filled. Two friends, two women hired for the evening, drinks and rooms and a city going on outside: Walter Hugo Khouri gives that arrangement ninety-three minutes and almost nothing to do, which is the design. The talk starts as banter and keeps going past the point where either man controls what it gives away. The women are not furniture here. The frustration is counted four ways, and their account of the transaction is the least sentimental one in the room. Khouri stays indoors with people who can afford the evening and finds them stranded anyway, which is the useful part: boredom between strangers is not idle time, it is crowded with everything nobody will say.

Attraction and revulsion arrive in the same man at the same time, and he cannot get them apart. He has money. She is a prostitute. What unsettles him is less her than the way his own reaction keeps changing shape while he watches it happen. Arnaldo Jabor filmed this in 1973 at a hundred and two minutes, long enough for a private confusion to become an expense other people pay, and pitched it high: rooms full of people saying the cruellest available version of what they mean, at a volume that keeps tipping toward farce without landing there. A Silver Bear came of it. The subject is not desire, which the film takes as given, but the labour a man of standing puts into deciding which of his feelings he is allowed to have.

A hardware store, an owner who is old, and behind the counter Fernandez, who knows what is in every drawer. That is the sum of his days until a woman enters them, and she does not come alone: there is a family attached, with a house, a routine and firm views on what a suitor is for. Leonardo Favio gives it eighty-seven minutes and very few rooms. A courtship conducted in front of witnesses leaves almost nothing unobserved, and the method is patience, small transactions, long stretches of nothing much, everyone involved seeming to know how this goes and waiting for Fernandez to catch up. Argentina, 1969, and hardly any of it happens outside the shop and the house. Loneliness here is not a mood but a schedule.

Letters begin arriving for the meekest man in the boarding house, and they are signed Rosaura. He paints, he keeps to himself, he has never been the subject of anything; now the other tenants have a story to follow, and they follow it into his room, his post and his affairs, which is what a boarding house is for. Mario Soffici lets the curiosity do the damage. Ninety-eight minutes of people improving on a small fact until it is too big to hold, and then the woman named in the letters is standing in the hall. It won a Silver Condor for Best Actress, which suits a film that assembles a woman almost entirely out of other people's talk before letting her speak for herself.
